blocks.text: Intermolecular Forces
Intermolecular Forces are the attractive and repulsive forces that act between neighboring molecules.

They are much weaker than the intramolecular bonds (like covalent or ionic bonds) that hold atoms together inside a single molecule. Even though they are weak, these forces control the physical properties of matter, such as boiling points, melting points, viscosity (how thick a liquid is), and surface tension.
Van der Waals Forces

The van der Waals force (sometimes van der Waals' force) is a distance-dependent interaction between atoms or molecules and one of the category of intermolecular force. Unlike ionic or covalent bonds, these attractions do not result from a chemical electronic bond; they are comparatively weak and therefore more susceptible to disturbance. The van der Waals force quickly vanishes at longer distances between interacting molecules.
Van der Waals forces were first postulated by the Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals in 1873 when he introduced his equation of state for real gases

blocks.text: Types of Intermolecular Forces
1. Forces Involving Fully Charged Ions
These interactions require at least one particle to have a permanent, full ionic charge. Here are the list of interactions organized from strongest to weakest:

items: Ion-Dipole Interactions - Interacting particles: A full ion and a polar molecule (e.g., Na⁺ dissolved in H₂O). The full charge of an ion strongly attracts the opposite partial charge of a permanent dipole.

Ion-Induced Dipole Interactions - A full ion and a nonpolar molecule/atom (e.g., Fe²⁺ binding to nonpolar O₂). The strong charge of an ion deforms the electron cloud of a neutral, nonpolar particle to force a temporary, induced dipole.

blocks.text: 2. Forces Involving Permanent Dipoles (Polar Molecules)
These forces occur between neutral molecules that possess a permanent asymmetry in their electron distribution.

items: Hydrogen Bonding - Polar molecules containing hydrogen bonded specifically to F, O, or N (e.g., H₂O, NH₃, HF). A uniquely strong, specialized subset of dipole-dipole attraction due to extreme electronegativity differences and the tiny size of the hydrogen atom.

Dipole-Dipole Interactions - Two polar molecules without specific H-bonding (e.g., HCl attracting another HCl, or SO₂). The permanent partial positive end of one molecule aligns with and attracts the permanent partial negative end of another.

blocks.text: 3. Forces Involving Temporary Dipoles (Nonpolar Particles)
These forces exist in all matter but are the only forces keeping nonpolar particles together.

items: London Dispersion Forces (Dispersion / Instantaneous Dipole-Induced Dipole) - All atoms and molecules, but specifically the sole force for nonpolar species (e.g., He, Ar, N₂, CH₄). Random, momentary fluctuations of electrons create a split-second "instantaneous dipole" in one molecule, which then induces a matching temporary dipole in its neighbor.

blocks.text: Formula for dipole moment
Measures the polarity of a chemical bond or a system of separated electrical charges. When to Use the Formula:

items: Measuring Bond Polarity: Calculate the strength of a polar covalent or ionic bond when you know the partial charge (Q) and the bond length (r).
Finding Percentage Ionic Character: Compare a theoretically calculated ionic dipole moment with the experimental value to see how ionic a covalent bond is.
Solving Physics Charge Problems: Find the separation distance or magnitude of paired opposite charges in an electric field.

Effects of IMFs on physical properties of substances

blocks.title: Proportionality of IMFs on different physical properties of substances

blocks.text: Why this is the case?

items: Melting / Freezing Point: Strong forces act like tight glue. You need more heat to melt the solid into a liquid. When cooling down, the strong forces easily lock molecules back into a solid at a higher temperature.

Boiling / Condensation Point: Strong forces hold liquid molecules tightly together. You need more heat to break them apart into a gas. When cooling down, those strong forces easily snap the gas molecules back into a liquid at a higher temperature.
Viscosity: Strong forces cause molecules to cling tightly to their neighbors. They cannot slide past each other easily, making the liquid thick and slow-flowing.
Surface Tension: Molecules at the surface are pulled tightly inward by the molecules beneath them. Stronger forces make this inward tug stronger, creating a tougher, more elastic
Vapor Pressure: Strong forces trap molecules tightly inside the liquid. Fewer molecules can escape into the air, creating fewer gas collisions and less pressure above the liquid.

studyMaterials.subject: Life and Career Skills
studyMaterials.title: Donald Super's Developmental Theory
studyMaterials.summary: Introduction to Donald Super and his Developmental Theory

blocks.text: 1. Topic Introduction

Donald E. Super (1910–1994), a prominent American counseling psychologist, introduced the Life-Span, Life-Space Theory under the core philosophy that career development is not a single, isolated decision. Instead, he conceptualized it as a lifelong, evolving process through which individuals express, implement, and continuously refine their self-concept within the world of work.

Building upon Eli Ginzberg’s earlier developmental framework which primarily addressed career choices up through early adulthood. Super significantly expanded the paradigm into a comprehensive, birth-to-death model. In doing so, he integrated developmental progression across chronological stages (life-span) with the fulfillment of multiple social and personal roles (life-space), establishing a holistic approach to understanding vocational behavior throughout an individual's entire life.
2. Core Constructs
1. Self-Concept

items: A person’s subjective view of themselves (abilities, personality, values, interests, and limitations).
Career choice is viewed as the tangible expression and practical implementation of one’s self-concept in the world of work.
Self-concept evolves with age, feedback, and life experience.

blocks.text: 2. Career Maturity

items: Readiness to cope with age-appropriate career developmental tasks (predominantly applied to adolescents and young adults).

blocks.text: 3. Career Adaptability

items: The set of skills which help individuals adjust to changing work environments, technologies, and job demands.

blocks.text: 3. Five Stages of the Human Lifespan
Super divided the human lifespan into five sequential major stages:
1. Growth (Birth to ~Age 14)
Developing self-concept, curiosity, basic work habits, and autonomy. Contains the following sub-stages:

items: Fantasy (4–10 yrs): Play-based role-playing and wish-fulfilling desires.
Interest (11–12 yrs): Liking certain activities determines aspirations.
Capacity (13–14 yrs): Abilities and realistic performance expectations are integrated into interests.

blocks.text: 2. Exploration (Ages ~15 to 24)
Testing self-concept in school, internships, part-time jobs, and social roles; identifying career direction. Contains the following sub-stages:

items: Crystallizing (15–17 yrs): Forming a general career direction or vocational identity.
Specifying (18–21 yrs): Choosing a specific occupational goal or academic major.
Implementing (21–24 yrs): Completing necessary training and entering entry-level employment.

blocks.text: 3. Establishment (Ages ~25 to 44)
Securing a foothold, demonstrating competency, and advancing within the chosen occupation. Contains the following sub-stages:

items: Stabilizing (25–30 yrs): Confirming the choice meets needs and demonstrating reliability in the role.
Consolidating (30s): Becoming established, recognized, and building positive professional reputation.
Advancing (Late 30s to 40s): Seeking promotion, leadership, higher earnings, or increased autonomy.

blocks.text: 4. Maintenance (Ages ~45 to 64)
Preserving achieved status, updating skills to stay relevant, and adapting to industry changes without necessarily pursuing rapid upward climbs.
5. Disengagement (Ages 65+)
Shifting priorities away from paid employment; planning and transitioning into retirement. Contains the following sub-stages:

items: Deceleration: Slowing down pace of work; delegating responsibilities.
Retirement Planning: Financial and lifestyle organization.
Retirement Living: Developing new pursuits, leisure, volunteerism, and family roles.

studyMaterials.title: Basic Rights of Employees
studyMaterials.summary: Introduction to the Basic Rights of every Employee

blocks.text: Core Framework of Philippine Labor Rights

Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution (Article XIII, Section 3) and the Labor Code of the Philippines (Presidential Decree No. 442, as amended), the State guarantees workers the right to security of tenure, humane conditions of work, a living wage, and participation in decision-making processes.
1. Security of Tenure and Due Process
An employee cannot be terminated without substantive grounds and procedural due process.
The following are valid causes for termination:

items: Just Causes (Employee Fault, Art. 297 [282]): Serious misconduct, willful disobedience (insubordination), gross and habitual neglect of duty, fraud or willful breach of trust, or commission of a crime against the employer or their immediate family.

Authorized Causes (Business/Health Grounds, Arts. 298–299 [283–284]): Installation of labor-saving devices, redundancy, retrenchment to prevent losses, closure/cessation of business, or incurable disease prejudicial to the employee or co-workers.

blocks.text: The Twin-Notice Rule

items: First Notice (Notice to Explain): Specifies the particular charges and grounds for termination, giving the employee a reasonable opportunity (at least 5 calendar days) to respond and submit evidence.
Second Notice (Notice of Decision): Communicates the final decision indicating that all circumstances involving the charge were considered.

blocks.text: 2. Working Hours, Overtime, and Rest Periods

rows: Art. 83, Labor Code of the Philippines
Maximum of 8 hours per day. Excludes a minimum 60-minute regular meal break (unpaid). Short rest periods (5–20 minutes) count as paid hours.
Art. 87, Labor Code of the Philippines
Work rendered beyond 8 hours on a regular day incurs an additional +25% of the hourly rate; work on rest days/holidays incurs +30%.
Art. 86, Labor Code of the Philippines
Additional +10% of regular hourly rate for work performed between 10:00 PM and 6:00 AM.
Art. 91, Labor Code of the Philippines
Compulsory consecutive rest period of not less than 24 consecutive hours after every 6 consecutive normal workdays.

blocks.text: 3. Statutory Monetary Benefits & Wage Protection

items: Minimum Wage: Dictated by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards (RTWPB) based on geographic location and industry sector.
13th Month Pay (P.D. 851): Mandatory benefit equivalent to $\frac{1}{12}$ of the total basic salary earned within a calendar year, payable on or before December 24.
Service Incentive Leave (Art. 95): At least 5 paid days per year for employees who have rendered at least one year of service (convertible to cash if unused).
Regular Holiday Pay: 100% regular pay even if unworked; 200% if worked.
Special Non-Working Days: "No work, no pay" applies unless company policy dictates otherwise; 130% if worked.
Non-Diminution of Benefits (Art. 100): Employers cannot unilaterally withdraw, eliminate, or reduce benefits that have ripened into an established, regular company practice.

blocks.text: 4. Collective Bargaining, Health, & Statutory Leaves
Philippine labor law heavily safeguards collective bargaining, occupational well-being, and family and health needs through specific statutory guarantees.

Under Article 253 [246] of the Labor Code, workers are granted the fundamental right to self-organization, enabling them to form, join, or assist legitimate labor organizations and negotiate a Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) without being subjected to employer unfair labor practices (ULP). Alongside union rights, Republic Act No. 11058 mandates strict Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) standards. This law guarantees every worker a safe and healthful working environment, requires employers to provide personal protective equipment (PPE) free of charge, and upholds the employee's right to refuse unsafe work without fear of retaliation.
In addition to workplace safety and collective action, the law provides comprehensive special statutory leaves designed to protect the health, welfare, and personal responsibilities of employees:

items: Maternity Leave (RA 11210): Grants 105 paid days for live birth (with an additional 15 days for qualified solo mothers) and 60 paid days in cases of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy.
Paternity Leave (RA 8187): Entitles married male employees to 7 paid days of leave for up to the first four deliveries of their legitimate spouse.
Solo Parent Leave (RA 8972, as amended by RA 11861): Provides 7 paid parental leave days annually to qualifying solo parents.
VAWC Leave (RA 9262): Provides 10 paid days of leave for female employees who are victims of Violence Against Women and Their Children.
Gynecological Surgery Leave (RA 9710 / Magna Carta of Women): Allows up to 2 months of fully paid leave for female employees following surgery caused by gynecological disorders.

studyMaterials.subject: Life and Career Skills
studyMaterials.title: Eli Ginzberg's Developmental Theory
studyMaterials.summary: Introduction to Eli Ginzberg and his Developmental Theory

blocks.text: 1. Overview & Historical Significance

Proposed in 1951 by an interdisciplinary team led by economist Eli Ginzberg, along with Sol W. Ginsburg (psychiatrist), Sidney Axelrad (sociologist), and John L. Herma (psychologist) in their seminal work, Occupational Choice: An Approach to a General Theory.

Prior to Ginzberg, career counseling relied primarily on the Trait-and-Factor theory (matching fixed personality traits or skills to job types at a single point in time). Ginzberg and his colleagues were the first to argue that occupational choice is a developmental process, evolving over time through distinct psychological stages.
2. Core Premises
Ginzberg’s original model was built on three foundational tenets:

items: Occupational choice is a process
The process is irreversible
Compromise is an essential aspect of every choice

blocks.text: 3. Stages of Career Development
1. Fantasy Stage
This stage is play-oriented and imagination-driven. Children adopt roles based on excitement, visible symbols, or heroic figures (e.g., superhero, astronaut, veterinarian, pilot).
2. Tentative Stage
During adolescence, individuals begin to evaluate their career options against internal and emerging external realities. This stage is divided into four sub-stages:

rows: Choices are driven by what the adolescent likes and enjoys doing.
Adolescents introduce personal competence and skill evaluation into the equation; they assess whether their abilities match their interests.
Individuals weigh personal values, lifestyle goals, and societal impact against career options.
The realization that immediate real-world decisions must be made (college selection, vocational school, or entering the workforce). Demands, independence, and external realities become urgent.

blocks.text: 3. Realistic Stage
Adolescents transition into early adulthood, narrowing their vocational scope into a defined profession through actionable commitments. This stage is divided into three sub-stages:

rows: Active investigation of remaining options; gaining firsthand experience through coursework, internships, or entry-level roles.
Commitment to a single general career field; the decision becomes clear and consolidated.
Final specialization within the chosen field, focusing on a specific role, branch, or graduate training program.

blocks.text: 4. Ginzberg’s Revision

Ginzberg revised his original theory to reflect societal changes and extended research. He later recognized that career development doesn’t limit itself to childhood and adolescence but that it is a life-long process. Ginzberg rescinded his claims that:

items: Career development comes to a close during the person’s early 20s when they start work.
Career development is irreversible.
The resolution of the choice always results in compromise.

blocks.text: 1. Topic Introduction
A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances (reactants) are changed into new substances (products) with different properties.
$Reactant → Product$
Example:
$2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O$
2. Signs of a chemical reaction
A chemical reaction can be identified using the following:

items: Change in color
Formation of a gas/bubbles
Formation of a precipitate
Change in temperature
Production of light
Change in odor

blocks.text: A chemical reaction causes the formation of a new substance. The atoms are rearranged into substances with new properties. This is in contrast to Physical Change, where no new substance is formed, with only the physical state changing
3. Types of Chemical Reactions
1. Synthesis Reaction

A synthesis reaction occurs when two or more simpler substances combine to form one more complex substance. It follows the pattern $A + B → AB$. The reactants may be elements or compounds, and the product is a single compound. For example, $2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O$, where hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water.
2. Decomposition Reaction

A decomposition reaction is the opposite of synthesis. It occurs when one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. It follows the pattern $AB → A + B$ and often requires energy such as heat, electricity, or light. For example, $2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂$, where water breaks down into hydrogen and oxygen.
3. Single Replacement Reaction

A single replacement reaction occurs when one element replaces another element in a compound. It follows the pattern $A + BC → AC + B$. The free element must be reactive enough to replace the element in the compound. For example, $Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂$, where zinc replaces hydrogen in hydrochloric acid.
4. Double Replacement Reaction

A double replacement reaction occurs when two compounds exchange their ions or parts to form two new compounds. It follows the pattern $AB + CD → AD + CB$ and usually happens when the reaction produces a precipitate, gas, or water. For example, $AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃$, where silver and sodium exchange partners.
5. Combustion Reaction

A combustion reaction occurs when a substance reacts rapidly with oxygen, usually releasing heat and light. Hydrocarbons commonly undergo combustion, producing carbon dioxide and water when there is enough oxygen. It follows the pattern $Fuel + O₂ → products$ For example, $CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O$, where methane burns in oxygen.

studyMaterials.subject: Effective Communications
studyMaterials.title: Academic and Technical Communication
studyMaterials.summary: Similarities and difference of Academic and Technical Communication

blocks.text: 1. Formal Communication

Formal Communication is the structured exchange of information, following predefined channels, hierarchy, and professional standards. It includes emails, reports, memos, letters, and other documented formats, ensuring clarity, authority, and consistency in workplace communication.
Formal Communication can be divided into Academic and Technical Communication.
2. Academic Communication

Academic communication is the formal exchange of ideas, information, and knowledge in educational and research settings. It includes essays, research papers, presentations, discussions, and academic reports.

It uses clear, organized, and formal language to present arguments, explain concepts, and support ideas with evidence. Its goal is to communicate information accurately and effectively to an academic audience.
Examples are:

items: Research paper
Academic essay
Thesis
Book review
Classroom discussion

blocks.text: 3. Technical Communication

Technical communication is the process of presenting specialized information clearly and accurately to a specific audience. It is commonly used in fields such as science, engineering, technology, and business.
It includes manuals, reports, instructions, proposals, and technical documents. Its main goal is to help readers understand information, solve problems, or perform tasks effectively.
Examples are:

items: User manual
Instruction guide
Technical report
Product specification
Safety instructions

blocks.text: 0. History

Did you know that Piecewise Function is only invented by one person? But rather during the 18th and 19th century a new view of functions emerged in tandem with the modern understanding of what a function actually was! Early on, mathematicians such as Leonard Euler actually eschewed the piecewise function as they thought for a function to be a function it had to be expressed with one algebraic expression. This proved problematic thought as real world forces such as the plucked string of a guitar have a discontinuous mathematical function at the center which eluded physicists at the time. It was not until 1837 however, that Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet formally defined a function as any rule that associates to each value of x one and only one value of y. These men then proceeded to use their function definitions in other fields, from the study of electrotechnics by Oliver Heaviside and his step function in the 1890s to Richard Courant and his Finite Element Method in 1943.
1. Topic Introduction

A piecewise function is a function that uses different rules or formulas for different values or intervals of its domain. Instead of having only one equation, it is defined by two or more equations, with each equation applying to a specific condition.

Piecewise functions are useful for representing real-life situations that change depending on certain conditions. For example, a delivery fee may have different rates depending on the distance, or a taxi fare may change after reaching a certain number of kilometers.
2. Parts of a Piecewise Function

rows: Value greater than zero but less than or equal to three

blocks.text: 3. Real-Life Application

A parking garage charges ₱40 for the first 2 hours of parking. If a vehicle stays for more than 2 hours but not more than 5 hours, the total parking fee is ₱70. For vehicles parked for more than 5 hours, the total fee is ₱100.
1. How much would a customer pay if they parked for 1.5 hours?
2. How much would they pay if they parked for 4 hours?
3. How much would they pay if they parked for 7 hours?
Intermolecular Forces are the attractive and repulsive forces that act between neighboring molecules.

They are much weaker than the intramolecular bonds (like covalent or ionic bonds) that hold atoms together inside a single molecule. Even though they are weak, these forces control the physical properties of matter, such as boiling points, melting points, viscosity (how thick a liquid is), volatility (tendency of a substance to evaporate), and surface tension.
Types of Intermolecular Forces
1. London Dispersion Forces

London Dispersion Forces are weak intermolecular forces caused by temporary uneven distributions of electrons in atoms or molecules. These temporary dipoles can attract nearby particles. They are present in all atoms and molecules, including nonpolar molecules, and generally become stronger as the number of electrons increases.
The London Dispersion Force affects the following properties:

items: Boiling Point
Melting Point
Viscosity
Surface Tension
Volatility

blocks.text: 2. Dipole–Dipole Forces
Dipole–Dipole Forces are attractions between polar molecules where the partially positive end of one molecule attracts the partially negative end of another.
Dipole–Dipole Forces affect the following properties:

items: Boiling Point
Melting Point
Solubility

blocks.text: 3. Hydrogen Bonding
Hydrogen bonding is a strong intermolecular force that occurs when hydrogen is directly bonded to nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), or fluorine (F) and is attracted to a nearby electronegative atom.
Hydrogen Bonding affects the following properties:

items: Boiling Point
Melting Point
Solubility

blocks.text: 4. Ion–dipole
Ion–dipole forces are attractions between an ion and a polar molecule, where the positive or negative ion is attracted to the opposite partial charge of the polar molecule.
Ion–dipole forces affect the following properties:

items: Solubility
Dissolving of ionic compounds in water

blocks.text: 5. Dipole–induced dipole

Dipole–induced dipole forces are weak attractions between a polar molecule and a nonpolar molecule, where the polar molecule temporarily distorts the electron cloud of the nonpolar molecule, creating an induced dipole.
Dipole–induced dipole forces affect the following properties:

items: Solubility
Boiling Point
Melting Point
Volatility

blocks.text: 6. Ion–induced dipole
Ion–induced dipole forces are weak attractions between an ion and a nonpolar molecule, where the ion distorts the electron cloud of the nonpolar molecule, creating a temporary dipole.
Ion–induced dipole forces affect the following properties:

items: Solubility
Boiling Point
Melting Point
Volatility

quizSets.subject: General Chemistry
quizSets.title: Intermolecular Forces & Physical Properties (Active Recall)
quizSets.desc: Master London dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, ion-dipole forces, and their effects on boiling points and vapor pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the primary condition required for **Hydrogen Bonding** to form between molecules?
questions.front: What is the primary structural condition required for **Hydrogen Bonding** to occur?
questions.back: A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom with small atomic radius ($\text{N}$, $\text{O}$, or $\text{F}$) interacts with a lone pair on a nearby $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$, or $\text{F}$ atom.
questions.hint: Think of the acronym: FON (Fluorine, Oxygen, Nitrogen).
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is an unusually strong dipole-dipole attraction (~20 kJ/mol) occurring exclusively when H is attached directly to Fluorine, Oxygen, or Nitrogen due to extreme polarity and small atomic radii.

questions.prompt: How does molecular size / molar mass affect the strength of **London Dispersion Forces (LDF)**?
questions.front: How does molecular size and molar mass affect the strength of **London Dispersion Forces (LDF)**?
questions.back: Larger molecules with higher molar mass have larger electron clouds, increasing **polarizability**, which produces stronger temporary dipoles and higher boiling points.
questions.hint: More electrons = easier to distort the electron cloud.
questions.explanation: Polarizability increases with the number of electrons and diffuse electron clouds, making induced dipole fluctuations significantly stronger in heavier molecules.

questions.prompt: How do water molecules orient themselves around a dissolved $\text{Na}^+$ cation versus a $\text{Cl}^-$ anion in aqueous solution?
questions.front: How do water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) molecules orient around a $\text{Na}^+$ cation vs a $\text{Cl}^-$ anion during hydration?
questions.back: Around $\text{Na}^+$, water orients its partially negative Oxygen atom ($\delta^- \text{O}$). Around $\text{Cl}^-$, water orients its partially positive Hydrogen atoms ($\delta^+ \text{H}$).
questions.hint: Opposite charges attract: $\delta^-$ toward $(+)$ and $\delta^+$ toward $(-)$.
questions.explanation: Ion-dipole forces dictate hydration spheres: cations interact with the negative dipole pole ($\text{O}^{\delta-}$), while anions interact with the positive dipole poles ($\text{H}^{\delta+}$).

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between Intermolecular Force (IMF) strength and **Vapor Pressure**?
questions.front: What is the relationship between Intermolecular Force (IMF) strength and **Vapor Pressure** at a given temperature?
questions.back: **Inversely proportional**: Stronger IMFs $\implies$ Fewer surface molecules can escape into gas phase $\implies$ **Lower Vapor Pressure** (and Higher Boiling Point).
questions.hint: If molecules stick tightly together, can they easily evaporate into vapor?
questions.explanation: Strong cohesive forces prevent molecules from entering the vapor phase, resulting in low vapor pressure and requiring higher thermal energy (higher boiling point) to boil.
